newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-LOVE WINS PGA CHAMPIONSHIP BY FIVE OVER LEONARD.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-LOVE WINS PGA CHAMPIONSHIP BY FIVE OVER LEONARD.

text.p: Davis Love outdueled British Open champion Justin Leonard in a brilliant final-round performance Sunday to win the PGA Championship by five strokes and claim his first major championship.

Love, who began the day tied with Leonard at seven under, a massive seven shots ahead of the rest of the field, was near flawless as he posted five birdies and just one bogey in the pressure-packed showdown at the season's last major.
"What a thrill," said Love. "That's the best I ever felt on a golf course for four days with so much pressure."
Love, 33, finished with his third four-under-par 66 of the tournament for an 11-under total of 269.
As Love walked up the 18th fairway to the cheers of the gallery, a stunning rainbow graced the sky while the sun came out after a sudden downpour had drenched the course.

After rolling in a birdie putt to punctuate his triumph, Love hugged his brother and caddie Mark, his wife and his mother in a tearful celebration at the home hole. Love's father, famed teaching pro Davis Love Jr, was killed in a plane crash in 1988.

"It's been a long time coming," an emotional Love said after hoisting the silver Wanamaker Trophy. "I've been close a few times, as we all know. I was finding it hard to get through the last three holes without breaking down."
Love's maiden major fittingly came at the PGA, the championship of the organization his father belonged to for so many years.

"To win this championship was a great thrill for the son of a PGA member," Love said. "I knew he would be especially proud not only because it's a major but also because it's the PGA. He played here in '74 and he played in four or five PGAs."
Victory brought Love a first prize of $470,000.

Leonard's sensational putting touch deserted him after three impeccable rounds on Winged Foot's greens, and errant drives also gave him trouble. He made four birdies Sunday but had five bogeys as well.
Leonard, who set a course record with a five-under-par 65 Saturday, shot 71 to finish at six-under 274.
Jeff Maggert won his fight for an automatic berth on the U.S. Ryder Cup team by firing a 65 to finish third at 276.
Maggert made six birdies against one bogey to jump past Tommy Tolles into the 10th spot in the Ryder team standings.
The only other player to finish under par was Lee Janzen, who led after two rounds. Janzen birdied the last hole for 69 and a one-under 279 total.
Alone in fifth was U.S. Ryder Cup captain Tom Kite, who shot 70 for even-par 280.
Tiger Woods and Phil Mickelson, playing in one of the day's glamor pairings, both closed with 75s for 286, six over par.

Love's 269 total at fabled Winged Foot was spectacular. In four U.S. Opens held at the classic course, the winners shot 294 (Bobby Jones in 1929), 282 (Billy Casper in 1959), 287 (Hale Irwin in 1974) and 276 (Fuzzy Zoeller in 1984).
"I'm surprised anyone could shoot so low on this golf course," Love said. "Winged Foot is a very special place. It's incredible to be put in with the other great champions."
Leonard, a good friend of Love's, said: "Davis played extremely well today. He never let up.
"He's a classy guy, he always has been. That makes up a little bit for my disappointment," added Leonard, who was trying to match Nick Price's 1994 feat of winning two successive majors.
Love was solid from the start, hitting fairways, getting it close on approaches and using unerring judgement on the speed of Winged Foot's notoriously fast, sloping greens.
Leonard's slide started quickly.
At the second hole, Leonard pushed his tee shot into the right rough, punched back into the fairway and took a bogey to end a string of 20 holes of par or better.
Love made it a two-stroke lead by curling in a birdie putt at the par-3 third hole.

Another bogey by Leonard after driving into the rough at the fourth hole made it a three-shot advantage for Love, who extended that with a birdie tap-in at the par-5 fifth after narrowly missing an eagle putt.
After another birdie, Love led by five shots at the turn, but saw his lead cut to three at the 12th, where he bogeyed after finding the rough, while Leonard made birdie to reach seven under par.
Leonard's last chance probably came at the 13th.
The Texan's tee shot at the par-3 hole gave him a good chance for birdie. Love, meanwhile, sent his tee ball wild left and into deep rough with very little green to work with.

Another two-shot swing would have shrunk Love's lead to one, and bogey looked likely for Love. But Love gently lobbed the ball out of the junk and nearly holed it, lipping out of the cup and then tapping in for par.
Leonard missed his birdie. The three-shot lead remained.
"That's the hole that really saved me," Love said. "It saved the tournament for me."
Love, who had posted five top-10s in majors since being runner-up at the 1995 Masters, won going away after that and got rid of the "best player never to win a major" moniker.
"I was proud to be put in that category," Love said. "It's also nice to get out of it."
